newsitem.title: INDIA: India heading for record tea output in 1996.
newsitem.headline: India heading for record tea output in 1996.

text.p: Indian tea production is expected to hit a record 785 million kg in 1996 (Jan-Dec) despite a decline in output in the southern states, planters and industry officials said on Tuesday.

"South India is trailing behind last year by six million kg but east and north-east is up by 40 million kg," said an official of the Calcutta-based Consultative Committee of Plantation Association (CCPA).
"This is enough to reach the target," said the official, who did not want to be identified.
The government and the industry had set a record tea output target of 785 million kgs in 1996.
The north eastern states of Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur Tripura, Nagaland and Mizoram and the eastern state of West Bengal account for about 75 percent of India's tea output.
The southern states of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka produce the rest.

Until October, south India's output was 148 million kg against 154 million kg in the same period last year. North Indian production was 511 million kg, up from 471 million in the same period last year.
India produced 659 million kg of tea in January-October against 625 million kg in the same period last year, officials said.
"We expect this gap to prevail in November and December. So it would be (the targeted) 785 million kg totally against 750 million kg last year," the official said.
Industry officials said timely monsoon rains in the northeastern states benefitted the tea crop.
They said frost during the initial months hit the southern Indian crop. Severe power cuts in the southern states also adversely affected the tea industry.
Traders said prices in the local markets had fallen due to low export and domestic demand.
"The high productivity unmatched by export and domestic demand has pulled down prices by five rupees per kg in the last two months," said a leading tea trader.
Industry officials said south Indian crop quality should be improved to be competitive in the domestic and global markets.

"When some Assam teas are sold at 95 rupees a kg, south Indian teas are struggling to get an average of 42 rupees a kg because of low quality," said Subodh Paul, vice president of Contemporary Tea Services, a leading tea auctioneer.
V. Ramaswamy, a senior official in Carrit Moran and Company, another leading auctioneer, said India must produce quality tea and it must be promoted as a health drink to be globally competitive.
"In the sophisticated western markets, the trend in 1997 will be towards gourmet tea, speciality tea and organic tea," Ramaswamy said.
